DU002-001001-:
Situated on the coast at the mouth of the river Delvin. This passage tomb is part of Bremore cemetery (Rynne 1960, 79, Mound I). It comprises a circular cairn which is heavily grassed over (max. diam. 29m; H 3.5m). Possible kerbstones on W side. Disturbance at NW may indicate the remains of a collapsed passage and chamber (Herity 1974, 209, 255).
Best preserved of the mounds (I-V), it appears the mound had been perfectly conical 'until the 1940s when the Board of Works took stone from it to paint Eire in white along the cliff edge of the headland-as part of the Emergency Defenses'. This is according to the current owners, whose father owned the land at the time, and told them this is how the interior of the mound was collapsed. However cartographic evidence indicates there may have been collapse/quarrying of the mound in the previous century.
Geophysical survey (Licence no. 06R0050) of the mound did not return specific structural detail (Gimson 2006, 10). It did however show a drainage pipe had been inserted immediately to the east.  The Bremore headland was also subject to a constraint study carried out by Margaret Gowen & Company Ltd. in advance of a proposed port. In addition fieldwalking and lithic analysis was undertaken for an MA study (Collins, 2007).
Compiled by: Geraldine Stout
Updated by: Christine Baker
Date of upload: 16 April 2015
This monument is subject to a preservation order made under the National Monuments Acts 1930 to 2014 (PO no. 27/1976).

Kerbstones were visible at N and S sides in the 1970s. Disturbed core material consists of water-rolled pebbles (Herity 1974, 209, 255). Geophysical survey (Licence no. 06R0050) of the mound did not return specific structural detail (Gimson 2006, 10). The area was also subject to a constraint study carried out by Margaret Gowen & Company Ltd. in advance of a proposed port. DU002-001005-:
Situated on the coast at the mouth of the river Delvin. Part of the Bremore passage tomb cemetery (Rynne 1960, 81, Mound V).  It comprises a low sub-circular mound (max. dims. 11.5m N-S; 8.5m E-W; H 0.75m) with two large stones visible on the N side. Listed as a passage tomb (Herity 1974, 209). Geophysical survey (Licence no. 06R0050) of the mound identified  a cairn of stones covering a possible central burial or cremation. Seven isolated magnetic responses are arranged around the circumference of the mound. These may be interpreted as small pits or areas of burning (Gimson 2006, 10). The area was also subject to a constraint study carried out by Margaret Gowen & Company Ltd. in advance of a proposed port. In addition fieldwalking and lithic analysis was undertaken for an MA study (Collins, 2007).

DU002-010----:
In a field of tillage near the shoreline. Shown on Duncan's map (1821) as a 'moat'. Located on headland north of Lowther Lodge. Extensive views of the coastline up to the Mourne Mountains to north,  Bremore tombs to south. Area c.20m EW x 20m NS of stones, slightly elevated in a field of no stone. Some stones appear water rolled (majority >0.30m diam.) granite, sandstone and smaller quartz stones. Local tradition of this being the site of a tomb-quite a lot of flint retrieved from these fields. A miniature stone axe was found in the immediate vicinity (pers coms. Kieran Campbell).

DU005-057002-:
Located on the landscaped open space of Cloich Choirneal housing estate in Balrothery Village. It is four-sided with a distinct E-W axis (H 1.5m; 2, L 1.25m; Wth 0.95m). There are a series of plough marks on the lower portion of its W face (Healy 1975, 17). Archaeological test excavation (01E0255) and monitoring (01E0371) were undertaken in advance of the housing estate development. In 2010 a flower bed was placed around the  standing stone obscuring its base.

DU005-177----:
A single lichen covered stone (1.12m h., 0.8m diam.) located on the crest of high ground with extensive views. Dump of stones around the base and some gradual ground build up due to surrounding intensive agriculture. Traditionally known as the ‘Ho’ or ‘Howe’ stone.

DU008-013001-:
Situated on a small headland south of Loughshinney village. Prior to c. 1838 the site comprised a circular cairn (diam. c. 30m) with a funnel-shaped entrance and a rectangular chamber (L 2.4m; Wth 1.8m). Human bones were found in the chamber and midden material containing a possible microlith (DU008-013003)-) was found underneath (Newenham 1838, 247; Flanagan 1984, 15). Two cist burials were found in the cairn and a third W of the kerbstones (DU008-013002-).The cairn was partially removed by land improvement in 1838, the remainder incorporated into a field boundary. Remains of this field boundary extend almost from the cliff edge for c. 21m NS. Large stones (> 1m diam.) and small stone cairn material are visible within the overgrown field boundary. One large boulder is out lying c.2m south-east of the field boundary. No markings or decoration visible on these stones. Magnetic gradiometry undertaken by the Discovery Programme (Licence 08R247) did not succeed in establishing a location for the passage tomb as a large part of the area had been subject to intensive ploughing.
Compiled by: Geraldine Stout
Updated by: Christine Baker
Date of upload: 15 December 2014

DU015-032----:
The tomb is ituated by a pathway under tree cover at the edge of Deer Park golf course at the foot of Muck Rock on the north side of Howth Head. There is an entrance in SE to a single chamber (L 2.6m; Wth 1.1m). This is indicated by two portals (H 2.75m and 2.45m respectively). The doorstone has partially collapsed into the chamber. The large roofstone (L 5.2m; Wth 4.2m; D 1.9m) still rests on the upper edge of the portals above the collapsed chamber (Borlase 1897, 2, 376-9; Ó Nualláin 1983, 82, 96).

DU021-044----:
Situated in a field of pasture at the base of the S slope of Saggart Hill. The stones are aligned NW-SE and are 1.3m apart. The SE stone is a three-sided granite pyramid (H 1.4m; 1.2-1.5m), the NW stone is a rectangular, granite, pillar (H 1.6m; L 1-1.3m; Wth 0.8-0.9m). Known locally as the 'Adam and Eve' stones (McDix 1899, 125-9).

DU021-090----: Situated in a field due S of Kiltalown House. This standing stone (Wth 0.48m; H 1.05m) is a squat, irregularly shaped block of granite with some quartz banding. It has been set up on its broad end, narrowing towards the top and is orientated roughly N-S towards Tallaght Hill. In October 1996 the stone was knocked over. It became apparent that it had been sitting on its flat base with no evidence for a socket (Swan 1998, 57).
DU022-033----:
Located in gently sloping pasture, W of the River Dargle. Three tall granite orthostats survive forming three sides of a chamber which opens to the SSE (H 2.7m; Wth 2.35m; D 2.3m). The E portal-stone leans on the doorstone. A fourth stone had been broken up c. 1876 (Ó Nualláin 1983, 82, 96; Borlase 1897, 2, 393-4). Excavations undertaken between 1984 and 1987 revealed an oval-shaped cairn and concentrations of charcoal and cremated bone associated with the orthostats. A secondary pit burial in the cairn contained an inverted Food Vessel accompanying a cremation (DU022-033002-). N of the orthostats were a series of pits and post-holes and a linear trench, which produced a Late Neolithic/Early Bronze Age stone and pottery assemblage (DU022-033003-). A bowl furnance dating to the Iron Age was also revealed in this area (Keeley 1986, 18; 1987, 14-15; 1989-90, 74). Monitoring of groundworks in the same field as 'The Brehon's  produced a sherd of coarseware pottery. The fill was burnt, and it is possible that some burning did occur within the pit (Reid 2000, 35).
Compiled by Geraldine Stout
Date of upload: 26th April 2012
DU024-005001-:
Situated on the N-facing slope of Saggart hill at a point known as Knockaniller. This is a chambered cairn, circular in form (diam. 13m; H c. 2m) defined by granite kerbstones (diam. 13m; H c. 2m). There is a quantity of quartz in the cairn collapse. An undifferentiated chamber extends NE-SW, narrowing at the N end (L 4m; Wth 1.7m). There are no roofing or sillstones visible. The covering mound has been truncated by a field boundary along the SW. There is furze cover over the S section of site (Kilbride-Jones, 1950, 314; Herity 1974, 256, Mount 1988, 16-17). This site lies to the NE of a passage tombs and a ring-barrow at Knockaniller (DU024-005002-, DU024-005003-).
Compiled by: Geraldine Stout and Padraig Clancy
Revised upload on: 6 July 2018

DU024-005002-:
Located on the N-facing slope of Saggart Hill at a point known as Knockaniller. This large kerbed cairn lies immediately to the S of another passage tomb (DU024-005001-). It is circular in form and round-topped (diam. c. 40m; H c. 5m). Now partly fern-covered with deep machine tracks running across the top. A townland boundary runs between it and passage tomb to the N. (Herity 1974, 256; Herity 2001, 27-29).

DU024-013----:
Situated to the E of the N81 and the river valley. A granite standing stone (H 2.3m) is situated at a break in slope, in a field of rough pasture on ground that falls away to the W. It has a trapezoidal-shaped ground plan (S 1.3m; N 0.95m; W 0.84m; E 1.3m). The S face has been decorated with c. 28 cupmarks largely concentrated in one area (average diam. 0.06m). Some of these form a petal-like pattern (Briley 1898, 173-4; Ua Broin 1957; Healy 1975, 1-19).

Revised upload ob: 6 July 2018
DU024-027002-:
Situated on a rise in a natural plateau on the NE side of Tallaght Hill. A stone circle comprised of a series of 14 irregularly spaced boulders of granite and conglomerate which appear to delimit rather than define a cairn (DU024-027001-).  There is a triangular-shaped granite boulder at W (H 1.5m; L 0.9m; Wth 0.6m) and a large recumbent conglomerate (H 1.05m; L 1.3m; Wth 1.2m) almost directly opposite. Mc Dix (1925, 26) mentions an inner circle of stones (diam. c. 2.7m) but this is not apparent at the time of inspection.

Revised upload on: 7 July 2018
DU024-028----:
Situated on a natural plateau on the NE side of Tallaght Hill which is in rough upland pasture. A stone circle indicated on the 1843 OS 6-inch map. There are no visible remains of the site. Further S are a number of irregular granite boulders in no apparent pattern. These stones are locally referred to as 'Horan's Stones', after Malachy Horan who was a resident of the area many years ago (Healy 1975, 1-19).
Compiled by: Geraldine Stout and Padraig Clancy
Revised upload on: 7 July 2018
DU024-030----:
The monument stands within a modern conifer plantation on a terrace on the E side of Knockannavea hill.  A passage tomb consisting of an incomplete circle of kerb-like boulders enclosing an area approximately 8m in diameter. At the centre is a hollow in which are exposed four stones, probably the remains of a burial chamber. These stones may probably be identified with those mentioned by McDix as forming part of a ‘smaller inner circle’ (McDix 1925, 126). Four boulders along the SE side were displaced in 1986 in the course of forestry work. This area was excavated in 1988 and the stones replaced in their original positions. No finds were recovered (Healy 1988). The monument appears to represent the denuded remains of a probable passage tomb. (Herity 1974, 123).I t was named ‘Cromlech’ on the first edition of the OS 6-inch map: this was changed to ‘Stone Circle’ on the 1937 edition.
Compiled by: Paul Walsh and Padraig Clancy
Revised upload on: 7 July 2018
DU024-034----:
The site is located in a clearing in Slievethoul Woods on the summit of Saggart Hill. A passage tomb comprises of a large circular, round-topped, chambered cairn (diam.22m; H 2.75m). There is a central hollow where cairn material has been robbed. The chamber extends E-W. There are four orthostats in position. The site is too overgrown to identify kerbstones but Herity (1974, 256) describes a single granite boulder visible near the base at N edge of a cairn (Healy 1975, 1-19). It lies c. 300m WNW of passage tomb (DU024-035----)

Situated on the W downslope of Seahan Mountain summit, on which stands a passage tomb (DU024:047----). A passage tomb comprises of a circular mound of gravel and stone (diam.8m; H 0.55m). This encloses a disturbed stone structure which has been interpreted as a possible cruciform chamber with a passage aligned NNW-SSE (Redmond and Mac Aonghusa 1994, 38). DU024-047001-:
Situated on the summit of Seahan Mountain from which there are extensive views of the Liffey valley, and the passage tombs at Mountpelier.  The passage tomb comprises of a circular round-topped cairn (diam.28m; H 4m). A trignometrical station has been placed on the top. There are no kerbstones visible but there is a ledge around the base which indicates their presence under the cairn material. Passage tomb (DU024:047002-) lies 7m to the NE and passage tomb (DU024:046----) lies to the SW. (Healy 1961, 128; 1975, 1-19; Herity 1974, 255-7; Redmond and Mac Aonghusa 1994, 36-9). According to the OS Letters (1837) this mountain was known to the local people as 'Suighchan' or the Seat (Herity 2001, 21). From it there are extensive views of the Liffey valley, and the passage tombs at Mountpelier.
Compiled by: Geraldine Stout and Padraig Clancy
Revised upload on: 7 July 2018
DU024-047002-:
Situated NE of  the summit of Seahan Mountain from which there are extensive views of the Liffey valley, and the passage tombs at Mountpelier. The passage tomb is much denuded and peat covered. It comprises a roughly circular cairn (diam.22m) which is defined by boulders, best preserved in the S and E. Many of the kerbstones have been displaced. There are indications of a passage, aligned N-S and a central square chamber (0.9m sq. ) defined by three orthostats at W (H 0.49m), E (H 0.7m) and S (H 0.57m). The chamber is covered by a slightly displaced capstone (Herity 1974, 256; Redmond and Mac Aonghusa 1994, 36-9).
Compiled by: Geraldine Stout and Padraig Clancy
Revised upload on: 7 July 2018
DU025-001001-:
This passage tomb and its adjacent companion (DU025-001002-) are located on the crest of Montpellier Hill, just SE of a ruinous hunting lodge called the Hell Fire Club (DU025-001003-).  The monument enjoys panoramic views N and E with those to the S and W somewhat restricted by forestry. These passage tombs are part of a cluster of passage tombs situated largely along the N and W perimeter slopes of the Dublin and Wicklow mountains.
The monument appears as a hollowed-out mound (dims. 18.8 N-S; 26m E-W; H 1.5m) enclosed by a shallow ditch with an external counterscarp bank running from E-W. It may have been re-configured into a ring-barrow at some time in prehistory. That portion of the monument at the NE adjacent to the Hell Fire Club is clearly robbed-out and in this quadrant the mound is flattened.
There were kerbstones, not apparent today, visible along the perimeter in the SE which were recorded first from the diaries of Austin Cooper, an 18th century antiquarian who visited the monument in 1779 (Herity 1974, 257; Price 1942, 66 Healy 1975, 1-19). Cooper writes “"On The Top of the Hill of Montpelier stands a house built by the late Mr. Connolly, it is all arched and is now entirely out of Repair. Upon the Top of this Hill formerly stood a Kaim, which was removed to make room for the house... behind the house are still the Remains of the Kaim, the Limits of it, were composed of large Stones set Edgeways, which made a sort of a Wall or Boundary of abt. 18 Inches high & withinside those, were the small stones heaped up. It is 34 yards Diameter or 102 in Circumfe. In the very Centre, is a large Stone 9 feet long, 6 feet broad & abt. 3 feet thick, not raised upon large Stones but lying low, with the Stones cleared away from about it. There are several other large Stones lying upon the Heap. About 60 yards S.W. of this Stands a single Stone, of abt. 5 feet high, but whether. it is a part of this Druidical Remains, or only put up there for the Cattle to scratch themselves (the Use it is now made of) I shall not positively say" (Price, 1942).
In 2016 a research excavation (16E0497) funded by Dublin South County Council took place with the purpose of assessing whether any archaeological features were present and what the nature of those deposits were. (Jackman 2016, 1-33). Two trenches were excavated ; Trench 1 15m x 2m orientated N-S running from the centre of the monument towards the external edge and Trench 2 10m x 2m orientated E-W  across the centre of the northern quadrant in the most disturbed part of the monument. Original cairn material was identified relating to the tomb construction by excavation.  The enclosing fosse which follows the edge of the monument was identified as a late robber trench probably associated with the quarrying of kerbstones as building material for the construction of the nearby Old Military Road at the beginning of the 19th century. Within layers of disturbed deposits were some  significant finds including a polished stone axehead and a decorated stone. Further analysis will determine whether this stone belongs with the corpus of megalithic art.
Compiled by: Margaret Keane
Revised upload on: 7 July 2018
DU025-001002-:
This passage tomb and its adjacent companion (DU025-001001-) are located on the crest of Montpellier Hill, just SE of a ruinous hunting lodge called the Hell Fire Club (DU025-001003-). DU025-002----:
Situated on sloping pasture above the Owendoher river valley. A single chambered tomb facing NW is formed by a massive granite roofstone (L 6.3m; Wth 3.15m; D 1.3m) which rests on a broken portal (H 2.44m). The other portal lies close by (L 4.4m; Wth 1.1m) (Borlase 1897, 2, 282-5; Ó Nualláin 1983, 82, 90; Turner 1983, No. 6). A drawing by Gabriel Beranger (1781) shows more stones around the monument than there are today (Ball 1906, 48-9).

DU025-005----:
Situated on the lower N slopes of Tibradden Mountain. A megalithic tomb shown on the 1906 revision of OS map  as a small hachured mound bounded on the W and S by a hachured embankment. Noted on the Cassini 6" edition as 'Dolmen (site of)'. Removed in the course of gravel quarrying. Not visible at ground level.

DU025-006----:
Situated on the grounds of Larch Hill on gently sloping pasture near the valley bottom W of Kilmashogue Mountain. A megalithic tomb in a collapsed condition with a ruined chamber facing uphill to the E. One of the portal stones, almost square in section, still stands (H 2.5m). The collapsed roofstone covers the chamber (L 3.8m; Wth 2.65m; D 0.7m). There are a number of large collapsed stones lying close to these structural stones. Borlase (1897, 2, 394-5) describes a circle of stones which is not apparent today (Turner 1983, 6-7; Anon.1914, 225-6; Price 1940, 124).
Complied by: Geraldine Stout and Padraig Clancy
Revised upload on: 8 July 2018
DU025-007001-:
Situated in a forest clearing on a level platform on the N slopes of Kilmashogue Mountain. From an account of this monument prior to the growth of forestry in the environs it commanded extensive views to the N, E and W (Kilbride-Jones 1953) .
This site comprises a gallery with a curved alignment ENE-SW (L 6m; Wth at SSW 1.8m; Wth at NNE 1.5m) divided into a main chamber and  an antechamber. It is enclosed by three lines of orthostats, forming a wedge-shaped plan. Only the N portion of the cairn survives (D. 0.80m) but it appears originally to be oval in form without an obvious kerb. To the S the remains of a kerb has been identified, as a curving arc of  stone-sockets, some with packing stones. The antechamber is composed of four orthostats and at the NE a portal stone with its main axis at right angles to the chamber matched with a similarly placed stone socket on the other side.  The chamber is defined by a rear back stone and front septal stone and orthostatic side walls. These consist of three parallel close-set rows of orthostats.  The side wall at the N leans sharply inwards.  According to the excavator this happened soon after construction. The floor of the chamber, which had been cut into the subsoil below the level of the antechamber floor was covered by a thin grey deposit with some cremated bone and charcoal and a single unworked piece of flint. The backstone was cut into subsoil below the level of the chamber floor while the septal stone which is well squared off sits on the chamber floor itself held in place between orthostats with cairn material.
Two secondary features, Cist 1 and Cist 2, at the centre of small sub-cairns,  are located in the NE quadrant of the cairn, to the rear of the gallery. Cist 1 is composed of four stones set on edge measuring internally 1.05m by 0.60m and is 0.45m in depth, covered by a domed capstone. The cist floor was fire-reddened and it contained a single upright food-vessel, near the NE side of the cist. Cist 2  lay to the S of Cist 1. It is composed of three small stones set on their long edges, and contained another food-vessel and quantities of cremated bone. Within the overall cairn material are another two dense concentrations of cairn material, in addition to those over the cists, possibly indicative of more secondary burials, as well as a small fireplace defined by stones and filled with powdered charcoal just NE of Cist 1.
A third secondary feature, Cist 3, is located in the ante-chamber. It comprises a circular area in a circular pit dug into the subsoil and lined by eight stones forming a polygonal cist with a single thick stone as a floor and with a capstone above. On the stone floor an inverted cinerary urn was placed containing large amounts of cremated bone (Kilbride-Jones 1953, 461-79; Healy 1975a 1-19; Turner 1983)
This is a National Monument in State Ownership (No. 493).
Compiled by: Geraldine Stout and Margaret Keane.
Uploaded on: 22 January 2018
DU025-021001-:
Situated in a forest clearing W of the site of a large enclosure (DU025-021002-) planted with trees. It was described as an irregularly shaped granite boulder (H. 3m) which terminates in a point at the top (Healy 1975, 1-19) but is now prostrate across a modern trackway to the crest of the hill.

DU025-022----:
Situated in a state forestry plantation on a slight summit overlooking the Glen between Cruagh and Mountpelier. A megalithic tomb consisting of an irregular low mound (Wth 7m) which contains a number of protruding upright slabs (Ó hÉailidhe 1978, 101-3). The chamber extends E-W, with a W-facing façade and entrance (L 6m; Wth 6m). It is defined by sidestones and one endstone. Running parallel to the sides are remains of a double revetment wall of upright slabs. There are traces of kerbstones in the NW. Both the cairn material and roofing slabs have been removed.
Compiled by: Geraldine Stout and Padraig Clancy
Revised upload on: 8 July 2018
DU025-025----:
Situated on the summit of Two Rock Mountain. This is a roughly circular flat-topped cairn (diam.27m; H 3m). There are two inclined kerbstones on the N side, c. 3m apart. According to the ITA Survey (1945) there were indications of a passage extending NW-SE axis. This is not apparent today (Price 1940, 124; Herity 1974, 209, 257).
Compiled by: Geraldine Stout and Padraig Clancy
Revised upload on: 8 July 2018
DU025-045----:
Located on the lower slopes of Two Rock Mountain in a clearing in the forest, the land falls from NW to SE and the views are totally restricted by trees. When this monument was excavated in 1945 prior to the growth of forestry (Ó Ríordáin and De Valera, 1951-3), it commanded extensive views to the S  and SE  but the aspect was restricted somewhat upslope to the N and limited to the W.
It had been described on the first and subsequent editions of the  Ordnance Survey maps as a ‘Giant’s Grave’.  When first documented the monument was classed as a tumulus (O’Dovovan, 1837) but the cairn was progressively robbed out to expose the tips of some orthostats of the chambered tomb below.  Prior to excavation it consisted of a high oval cairn (L. 17m, Wth. 12m, H, 2m) with the general location of the facade and gallery visible (Borlase 1897, 2, 385-7).  Borlase records, quoting O' Curry: " 'I doubt' says he 'that we have encountered a pagan grave as perfect in any other county yet examined' "(ibid, 385).
Excavation revealed a ‘classic’ wedge tomb set within a heel-shaped cairn. Centrally placed within the cairn  the wedge comprises a gallery aligned E-W divided into three sections, an ante chamber, a main chamber and an eastern end chamber. The horseshoe-shaped cairn, defined by very closely spaced and well-matched kerbstones, has a straight façade at the W onto which the gallery opens. An upright  (H. 1.2m) flanking the N side of the entrance is the only in situ façade orthostat in place.  Judging from the layout of stone sockets it appears that the façade both to the N and to the S of the gallery curves slightly towards the revetments. According to the excavators the front facade bore the main thrust of the loading from the cairn material.  The cairn is composed of stones with a filling of clean yellow sand. Within the cairn is what the excavators describe as a complex series of revetments parallel to the kerb and to the façade. Lying loose on the southern side of the cairn between the kerb and the internal revetment is a granite boulder (L .70cms, W 40cms, D 20cms) with seven small cupmarks on one surface (DU05-089----.)
The tomb at Ballyedmonduff is important in that it displays a fairly complete kerb which is largely intact. The original kerb consisted of 25 kerbstones (H. 0.5-1.0m) 17 of which were in place, the remainder indicated by a 0.4m deep construction trench.  At the front the kerb curves around in a continuous arc to form the outer revetment of massive orthostats (H.75m – 1.5m).  These are set with an inward inclination and with curved outer edges to the stones and straight inner edges. Running parallel to this yet converging at the very large revetment backstone is an inner revetment, absent for a short length to the S but clearly expressed at the N.
The ante-chamber is 1.5m (E-W) and .75m (N-S), its sides defined by two orthostats at the N and by a single large orthstat at the S, all damaged by stone cutters. Horizontally laid slabs supplement the height of lower orthostats providing a levelled overall ante-chamber height suggestive of a lintelled roof arrangment. …
DU025-046----:
Situated on the lower S slopes of Two Rock Mountain. A stone circle comprised of a circular area defined by seven orthostats (H c. 1m) and ten more stones only partially exposed. This site was first identified by Healy in 1967 (1975, 1-19). Unfortunately it was planted with trees in 1972 leaving no visible remains at ground level.
Compiled by: Geraldine Stout and Padraig Clancy
Uploaded on: 28 July 2018
DU025-047002-:
Situated on the upper crest of a hill above the old chapel in Glencullen village. A standing stone comprising of a granite orthostat (H 1.75m) is square in plan (dims. 0.65m x 0.65m) and has a pointed top (Healy 1975, 1-19; Turner 1983, 14). Shown on the 1843 OS 6-inch map. Situated c. 6m NE of a barrow (DU025-047001-) on the upper crest of a hill.
Compiled by: Geraldine Stout and Padraig Clancy
Revised upload on: 28 July 2018
DU025-047003-:
Cairn of possible megalithic tomb unclassified known locally as 'Ossian's Grave' was recorded by James Kyle in 2003 while carrying out an archaeological survey of the lands at Newtown and Glencullen.  He correctly suggested that the location of the cairn listed in the Dublin RMP as DU025-047003- and was marked in the wrong location.   Cairn of possible megalithic tomb described by James Kyle as follows; 'Located 100m southeast of the Rathín, to the immediate west of a mature Hawthorn tree were the apparent remains of a robbed out megalithic tomb, which is suggested to be the tomb referred to as Ossian’s Grave by the 1837 O.S. letters and folklore. The monument is roughly kite/wedged shape in plan, with surviving kerb stones evident around much of the perimeter of the cairn. The tip of the wedge is oriented to the southeast and this would appear to suggest the most likely candidate for the original entrance to the tomb was at the wider, northwest end. The overall impression from the remains of this megalithic tomb suggests that it was possibly a wedge tomb-type megalith, and it was depicted by only the 1837 O.S. mapping and it is not listed as an RMP or present on the SMR or the 1910 mapping' (Kyle 2023, 21-2).
Compiled by: Caimin O'Brien based on details provided by James Kyle
DU025-050----:
Situated at the edges of a golf course,  on a gentle NW facing slope, just S of the crossroads at Glencullen with extensive views to the N, good views E and W but restricted upslope to the S. This is a rectangular block of quartz, narrowing a little towards its base (H 1.85m; L 1m; Wth 0.7m) orientated NE-SW. It is  unusually blocky in its shape as most monuments of this class are much thinner than they are long and regularly have a pointed or angled top rather than the flat top of this regular block. There are no packing stones but the standing stone is well grounded.  Known locally as 'Queen Mab' but described in the School’s Manuscript Collection as marking the grave of a chief who lived in the district (Healy 1975, 1-19; Turner, 1983, 14).
This monument is a National Monument in State ownership (Nat. Mon. 276).
Compiled by: Geraldine Stout and Margaret Keane
Revised and updated on: 5 March 2018
DU025-051----:
Known locally as the 'Shed Stone' this tomb is situated on the N bank of a stream at the head of Glenasmole valley. It comprises of an oblong boulder (L2.30m, Wth 1.90m; 0.75m) single chamber (int. dims. L 1.25m; Wth 0.9m-1.45m; H 1.35m) supported by two granite portal stones (H 1.08m and 0.55m respectively) and a backstone of granite that carries a massive capstone (L 2.1m; Wth 1.6m; D 0.6m). Loose boulders lie around the perimeter of the tomb (McDix 1925, 122; Price 1940, 123; Healy 1961, 115-6)
Compiled by: Geraldine Stout and Padraig Clancy
Revised upload on: 28 July 2018
DU025-080----:

He was 9 feet7 inches high and weighed 44 stone' (Healy 1961, 115). Precise location unknown.

DU025-087----:
Situated on a gentle E facing slope in undulating pasture. A cursus consisting of a u-shaped earthwork is visible on an aerial photograph aligned approximately NW–SE; the curve of the U is at the SE. It is defined by a low bank and external fosse that encloses an area c. 125m by 45m. The precise nature of this earthwork is unknown and the possibility that it could be the remnants of a cursus-type monument cannot be excluded.

DU026-007----:
This very impressive portal tomb is located on the valley floor of a steep-sided glen close to a stream. A massive wedge-shaped granite roofstone (L 5.1m; Wth 4.5m; D 1.75m) covers a chamber (int. dims. L 3.1m; Wth 1.42m) and antechamber facing west. It rests on the two front portal stones (H 2.6m and 2m respectively) and three sidestones. A doorstone separates the main chamber from the antechamber. There are some granite boulders at the rear of the tomb wall which may have been part of an additional chamber (Borlase 1897, 2, 390-92; Ó Nualláin 1983, 96; Turner 1983, 5). There are two deep depressions on the upper surface of the roofstone, with groves leading to the corner of the stone. It has been suggested that this be an original drainage feature.
The monument was taken by Guardianship into State Care (Nat Mon 291)
Compiled by: Geraldine Stout and Margaret Keane
Uploaded on: January 15 2017
DU026-019----:
This portal tomb is located on a SW-facing slope in rock-strewn pasture.  In recent years there has been considerable land clearance in its immediate environs. Two portal-stones, which are angled forwards to the W, and a blocking stone form the entrance to a long rectangular chamber (L 4.5m; Wth 2.6m; H 1.25m). The capstone is massive (L 6.5m; Wth 5.3m; D 1.55m) thickest at the leading edge and  sloping sharply to a ground-fast rear stone at E. The chamber, which opens to the W was briefly excavated by Marcus Ó hEochaidhe, who found a chert arrowhead, three hollow scrapers and an end scraper  - all tools diagnostic of the Early Neolithic period (Corlett 2012; Herity 1964, 134-9; O'Neill 1852 42; Ó Nualláin 1983, 82, 96; Turner 1983, 6;).
This monument was subject to a preservation order made under the National Monuments Acts 1930 to 2014 (PO no. 47/1936) and was subsequently taken into Guardianship under the National Monuments Acts 1930 to 2014  (National Monument 343).
Compiled by:  Geraldine Stout and Margaret Keane
Uploaded on: 15 January 2017
DU026-024----:
Located on a ridge overlooking the Bride's Glen to the S. A roughly oval-shaped cairn (L 14m; Wth 12m; H 1.2m) orientated E-W. The kerbstones are visible along the N and S sides. The cairn narrows towards the E and curves inwards to create a heel-shaped appearance. There are indications of a straight façade at the W end (Fanning 1974, 151-3). Excavations close by in 2000 produced a finely polished, broken stone axe with pecking on its sides, possibly of dolerite, (Seaver & Keeley 2002, 12-14 ).
Compiled by: Geraldine Stout and Padraig Clancy.
Revised upload on:  14 April 2018.
DU026-030----:
The portal tomb is situated in a low-lying green area on a housing estate at Ballybrack off the Shanganagh-Bray road. This simple portal tomb comprises a large sloping granite roofstone (L 2.2m; Wth 2.05m; T 1.2m) resting on two portal stones and two sidestones (portals H 1.55m and 1.4m respectively). The chamber faces E (L 1.89m; Wth 0.76m). There are no traces of a covering cairn.  It is known as the 'Shanganagh Dolmen' (Borlase 1897, 2, 392-3; Ó Nualláin 1983, 82, 96; Turner 1983, 5).
Tomb described in 1852 by Henry O'Neill as follows; 'This is usually called the Shanganagh dolmen.  The supporting-stones are four in number, two One of them is broken off in the middle, and the one opposite to it has fallen in. On these the covering-stone rests. It is nearly 7 feet 6 ins. [2.3m] square, by about 3 feet [0.9m] thick. The under side is, as usual, nearly flat. The weight of the stone is probably about 12 tons. The chamber lies E. and W., and measures 6 feet 7 ins. [2m] long by 2 feet 6 ins. [0.76m] wide. It was probably 5 feet [1.5m] high. The floor is of clay, and the material of the dolmen granite' (Borlase 1897, 392-3).
To see a 3D model of this monument visit https://skfb.ly/oJtSp
Compiled by: Geraldine Stout and Padraig Clancy
Revised by: Caimin O'Brien
Date of revised upload: 14 July 2023
DU026-042001-:
This megalithic tomb is located in pasture on a low SW-facing slope above the Glencullen River. The site comprises a flat-topped, furze-covered cairn (diam.32m; H 1.5-2m) with a possible chamber SW of centre, which is indicated by a standing stone (DU028-042002-). The cairn is partly truncated by a boundary wall. There is a large depression in the S half of the cairn. In the centre of the cairn there is a gallery aligned NW-SE (Wth 1.7-3.5m, L 1.9m). It is formed by five stones. In the 1970s there were three large granite slabs visible (Healy 1975, 1-19). A sketch map accompanying the OS Letters in 1837 show the site as a 'Giant's Grave' and an accompanying note mentions that 'There was a cromleac here but is now destroyed' (Herity 2001, 16). It is listed by Powell (1941, 21-23) as a gallery grave.
This monument is subject to a preservation order made under the National Monuments Acts 1930 to 2014 (PO no. 157/1940).
Compiled by: Geraldine Stout and Padraig Clancy.
Revised upload on:  15 April 2018.

DU026-059----:
This impressive tomb is located behind a field boundary in pasture at the foot of Carrickgollogan with views onto Sugarloaf Mountain. It comprises a rectangular chamber (int L 3.6m; Wth 1.4m; max. H 1.5m) which faces NE and is formed by four regular granite slabs set on their narrow axis. A large capstone (L 2.3m) covers the NE end of the chamber. It tilts towards the S as it is resting on the two larger front slabs, which vary in height. A tree stump blocks the rear of the chamber. (Borlase 1897, 2, 392; Healy 1975, 1-19; Turner 1983, 10).
Compiled by: Geraldine Stout and Padraig Clancy.
Revised upload on:  21 April 2018.
DU026-118----:
This recently discovered standing stone is located on a hillslope in pasture adjacent to Brenanstown House. It is formed of granite (H 1.15m; Wth 0.4m). Two small fragments of cremated bone were found directly in front of this stone when it was excavated in 1993 (Carroll 1994, 13). The stone had been set in a pit (diam. 0.8m) and was supported by smaller packing stones.
Compiled by: Geraldine Stout and Padraig Clancy.
Revised upload on:  21 April 2018.
DU026-132----:
Excavations along the Bord Gáis Pipeline between Carrickmines and Bray (licence no. 98E0445) revealed the remains of a multi-phased site incorporating a megalithic structure: this had been erected into a pre-existing fulacht fia. It was described by O'Neill (2000) as follows: 'The main components of the megalithic structure are a gallery of roughly parallel side-walls, orientated on an east-west axis, and a closely set outer walling. The stones are set within an irregular mound rather than sockets. Two buttress stones are present towards the eastern end of the gallery, where they rest against the outer walling. Neither could be definitely claimed to be functional. The gallery and the mound material around the orthostats were not excavated, leaving these features in their original position. There was a gap in the mound at the eastern end of the gallery, identifying this end as the front of the structure. The western end of the gallery is sealed by a low orthostat, and the whole structure had been placed within an artificial depression. This had been excavated into sloping ground. The orthostats in the northern wall of the gallery were noticeably higher than those in the southern wall. Traces of a cairn were present around and within the western end of the gallery. There were no surviving traces of a capstone. Externally the gallery is some 2.35m long and measures 3.4m across at the eastern end and 1.5m across at the western end. Internally it is 1.95m long, tapering from 1.42m across at the eastern end to 0.96m across at the western end. The mound surrounding the gallery was not fully examined as the eastern end lay beyond the limits of the site, where it is likely to have been heavily disturbed by a field boundary ditch. Its maximum identifiable width was 14m, and it was at least 9m long. The gap in the eastern end of the mound was 2.14m wide and was at least 1.65m long. It was positioned directly in front of the opening at the eastern end of the gallery.' While the design of the gallery has obvious affinities with many of those in the wedge tomb class, to which it was assigned by the excavator, the lack of any burial remains coupled with the atypical orientation, must caution against it being accepted as a definite example.
Image: DU026-132----_01. The monument in the course of excavation. Photograph looking east.
Compiled by: Paul Walsh
Date of upload: 27 July 2017
